result.markdown: --- title: "Derivatives" subtitle: "ConvolutionInterpolations.jl against Interpolations.jl, BSplineKit.jl and Dierckx.jl" engine: julia --- The first three derivatives of a difficult function from uniformly spaced samples: the analytic derivatives of the convolution kernels against those of the cubic B-spline of Interpolations.jl (first and second only, which is what it offers), the B-spline interpolants of BSplineKit.jl, and the quintic FITPACK spline of Dierckx.jl. First the accuracy as the grid is refined, then the time to evaluate a first derivative, and finally the time each method needs to reach a given accuracy in it. ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Packages, the methods, and the test function"} using ConvolutionInterpolations import Interpolations # qualified: exports `interpolate`, as BSplineKit does import BSplineKit import Dierckx using Chairmarks, Printf, Random, CairoMakie runge(x) = 1 / (1 + 25x^2) # Runge's function function drunge(x, m) # its m-th derivative, m = 1, 2, 3 s = 1 + 25x^2 m == 1 ? -50x / s^2 : m == 2 ? 50 * (75x^2 - 1) / s^3 : 15000x * (1 - 25x^2) / s^4 end xr = range(-1, 1, length = 2001) # fine points for measuring the error # each method maps (x, y, m) to a callable m-th derivative, or `nothing` where it has none function interpolations_derivative(x, y, m) m > 2 && return nothing # Interpolations.jl offers gradient and hessian s = Interpolations.scale(Interpolations.interpolate(y, Interpolations.BSpline(Interpolations.Cubic(Interpolations.Line(Interpolations.OnGrid())))), x) m == 1 ? (p -> Interpolations.gradient(s, p)[1]) : (p -> Interpolations.hessian(s, p)[1]) end bsplinekit_derivative(k) = (x, y, m) -> begin S = BSplineKit.interpolate(x, y, BSplineKit.BSplineOrder(k)) BSplineKit.Derivative(m) * S # the spline's m-th derivative, itself a spline end dierckx_derivative(x, y, m) = (spl = Dierckx.Spline1D(collect(x), collect(y); k = 5); p -> Dierckx.derivative(spl, p; nu = m)) convinterp_derivative(kernel, maxm) = (x, y, m) -> m > maxm ? nothing : convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = kernel, derivative = m) methods = [ "Interpolations.jl cubic" => interpolations_derivative, "BSplineKit k=4" => bsplinekit_derivative(4), "BSplineKit k=8" => bsplinekit_derivative(8), "Dierckx k=5" => dierckx_derivative, "ConvInterp :a4" => convinterp_derivative(:a4, 1), "ConvInterp :b5" => convinterp_derivative(:b5, 3), "ConvInterp :b7" => convinterp_derivative(:b7, 5), ]; ``` ::: ## Convergence The largest error of each derivative against the exact one, as the number of samples doubles. A method appears in a panel only if it provides that derivative order: ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The convergence study"} ns = [41, 81, 161, 321, 641, 1281] hs = 2 ./ (ns .- 1) errs = Dict((name, m) => Float64[] for (name, _) in methods, m in 1:3) for n in ns x = range(-1, 1, length = n) y = runge.(x) for (name, meth) in methods, m in 1:3 d = meth(x, y, m) d === nothing && continue push!(errs[(name, m)], maximum(abs.(d.(xr) .- drunge.(xr, m)))) end end fig = Figure(size = (800, 900)) axes = [Axis(fig[m, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xreversed = true, title = "derivative order $m", xlabel = "spacing h", ylabel = "largest error") for m in 1:3] for (name, _) in methods, m in 1:3 isempty(errs[(name, m)]) && continue scatterlines!(axes[m], hs, max.(errs[(name, m)], 1e-17); markersize = 8, label = name) end for m in 1:3 Legend(fig[m, 2], axes[m]) # each panel lists the methods it has end fig ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: | observed order | derivative 1 | derivative 2 | derivative 3 | |:--|--:|--:|--:| | Interpolations.jl cubic | 1.00 | -0.00 | — | | BSplineKit k=4 | 2.97 | 2.00 | 1.00 | | BSplineKit k=8 | 7.28 | -0.81 | -0.58 | | Dierckx k=5 | 5.00 | 4.00 | 2.96 | | ConvInterp :a4 | 2.99 | — | — | | ConvInterp :b5 | 5.63 | 4.39 | 3.99 | | ConvInterp :b7 | 6.04 | 4.99 | 3.94 | Every method loses about one order per derivative: the cubic ones from 4th order down to a piecewise-constant third derivative, Dierckx's quintic and `:b5` from 6th, BSplineKit at order 8 and `:b7` from their interpolation order. The rounding floor of a derivative rises with the number of samples, as $1/h^m$, which is the price of differentiating sampled data and the same for every method. ## Query time Evaluation time per point of the first derivative, at a million random points on a grid of a thousand samples, each derivative built once and evaluated in one broadcast: ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The timings"} rng = MersenneTwister(1) x1 = range(-1, 1, length = 1000) y1 = runge.(x1) p1 = rand(rng, 1_000_000) .* 1.98 .- 0.99 rows = map(methods) do (name, meth) d = meth(x1, y1, 1) t_query = (@b $d.($p1)).time / length(p1) (name = name, t_query = t_query) end; ``` ::: | | first derivative, per point | |:--|--:| | Interpolations.jl cubic | 29 ns | | BSplineKit k=4 | 49 ns | | BSplineKit k=8 | 55 ns | | Dierckx k=5 | 997 ns | | ConvInterp :a4 | 6 ns | | ConvInterp :b5 | 9 ns | | ConvInterp :b7 | 12 ns | A derivative of a convolution interpolant is the same stencil sum with the differentiated kernel's weights, so it costs what the interpolant costs. A spline derivative is a spline of one degree lower, evaluated like any spline; Interpolations.jl's `gradient` assembles the derivative from the B-spline's pieces at each call. ## Time to accuracy As on the [interpolation page](interpolation.qmd): for each method and each grid of the convergence study, the time to construct the first derivative and evaluate it at a hundred thousand points, against its error on that grid. ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The work–precision study"} pw = rand(rng, 100_000) .* 1.98 .- 0.99 # the evaluation workload times = Dict(name => Float64[] for (name, _) in methods) for n in ns x = range(-1, 1, length = n) y = runge.(x) for (name, meth) in methods push!(times[name], (@b begin d = $meth($x, $y, 1); d.($pw) end).time) end end fig = Figure(size = (800, 420)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xlabel = "time to construct and evaluate the first derivative at 10⁵ points [s]", ylabel = "largest error") for (name, _) in methods scatterlines!(ax, times[name], max.(errs[(name, 1)], 1e-17); markersize = 8, label = name) end Legend(fig[1, 2], ax) fig ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: The picture is the interpolation page's, one order down: the curves are nearly vertical, so each method's position is its cost per point and its depth is what its order buys, and the kernels are first to any accuracy of the derivative down to its rounding floor.
